title: Federal Court Postpones Rule Ending Duration of Status for Student Visas
excerpt: A federal judge in Massachusetts issued a nationwide injunction one day before a DHS rule was set to replace open-ended duration-of-status admissions with four-year caps for F and J visa holders — keeping the old system alive while the government appeals.
body:
• A federal judge in Massachusetts issued a nationwide injunction on September 14, 2026 — one day before it was to take effect — postponing a DHS rule that would have ended duration-of-status admissions for F, J, and I visa holders.
  • The blocked rule, published July 17, would have replaced open-ended D/S with fixed periods: four years for F and J students and exchange visitors, 240 days for I media visa holders, and cut the post-study grace period from 60 to 30 days.
  • For students in the U.S. now, nothing changes: D/S remains in force, I-20s and DS-2019s are issued as before, and no USCIS extension filings are required. Anyone re-entering the U.S. should verify admission terms on their CBP-issued I-94 record.
  • The pause is not permanent: the government appealed to the First Circuit on September 30 and seeks an expedited appeal, so the rule could return with little warning.

A federal judge in Massachusetts has preserved the decades-old duration-of-status system for more than a million international students, blocking — at least for now — a Department of Homeland Security rule that would have imposed fixed time limits on student and exchange-visitor stays. Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts granted a nationwide preliminary injunction on September 14, 2026, one day before the rule was to take effect, according to analyses by McGuireWoods and Fredrikson & Byron.

Context & Background

Duration of status is the system under which international students have been admitted to the United States for decades. Rather than being stamped in for a fixed number of years, an F-1 student is admitted for the full length of their academic program as listed on their Form I-20 — plus authorized practical training and a grace period — so long as they remain enrolled and in status. DHS tracks these students through the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS).

The July 17, 2026 final rule would have scrapped D/S entirely: four-year caps for F and J nonimmigrants regardless of program length, 240 days for I visa holders for foreign media, and discretionary USCIS extension filings for anyone needing more time — including doctoral students whose programs routinely exceed four years, with no administrative appeal from denials. The rule also restricted school transfers and changes of educational objective and added hurdles to Optional Practical Training and STEM OPT. DHS received nearly 22,000 public comments during rulemaking and, per McGuireWoods, disregarded concerns about enrollment deterrence and academic incompatibility.

Impact & Analysis

In Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Judge Saylor found the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim that the rule violated the Administrative Procedure Act: DHS had likely failed to conduct a proper cost-benefit analysis, meaningfully consider less restrictive alternatives, or respond to significant public comments — and had failed to show a rational connection between the rule and its stated goals of national security and fraud prevention, relying instead on anecdotal evidence of visa overstays.

"The rule's likely effect on higher education and the U.S. economy would be catastrophic."

— Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

The court also found that letting the rule take effect would cause immediate, irreparable harm to the roughly 1.2 million international students it would touch. Common App data cited in the case showed international applications to U.S. colleges already fell 9% for 2026-27, with applications from India down 14%, according to Collegedunia's summary of the record. For now, practitioners advise universities and employers to treat the old framework as controlling for all status, travel, and filing decisions — the court denied full vacatur without prejudice, so the injunction is a reprieve, not a verdict.

Diaspora Angle

Indian students stand among the largest beneficiaries of the ruling. Roughly 352,000 Indian students were in the United States as of early 2026, per DHS data cited by Collegedunia, making India the single largest source of international students. The blocked rule's four-year cap would have hit them especially hard: doctoral candidates, STEM master's students relying on 24-month OPT extensions, and students transferring programs would have faced discretionary USCIS adjudications mid-course, with denials carrying no internal appeal. For now, students keep D/S, the 60-day grace period, and existing OPT pathways without new filings.

"The judge recognized the harm the measure would cause to international students, universities and the economy."

— Miriam Feldblum, head of the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration

What's Next

The fight continues on two tracks. On September 30, the government filed a notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit — the appeal does not lift the injunction or revive the rule. At an October 2 status conference, the government said it would seek an expedited appeal and asked to pause district-court proceedings, while the plaintiffs urged a prompt final judgment so both tracks could proceed together; both sides were to file positions on next steps by October 9, per the Presidents' Alliance tracker.

The bottom line: duration of status remains the law of the land nationwide, but the rule is postponed, not dead. A First Circuit reversal could arrive with little advance notice. Students should watch the case and keep SEVIS records and I-94s clean — while remembering the administration intends to fight this to the end.
